entries.meaning: I have sung, as my understanding allowed, the incomparable and lovely love of the townspeople and Bharata. Now hear the supremely holy deeds by which the Lord delighted gods, human beings and sages in the forest. One day Rāma gathered lovely flowers, fashioned ornaments with his own hands, respectfully adorned Sītā with them, and sat beautifully upon a crystal rock. Indra's foolish son assumed a crow's form and tried to test Rāma's strength—like an ant wishing to sound the ocean. He struck Sītā's foot with his beak and fled; when blood flowed, Rāma understood and set a blade of grass to his bow as an arrow. Though Rāma is infinitely compassionate and always loves the helpless, that foolish abode of faults came and practised deceit against him.

Charged by the mantra, the Brahmā-arrow sped after the fleeing, terrified crow. Jayanta resumed his own form and went to his father, but no one shelters one who has turned against Rāma. Despair and dread arose in him, as in the sage Durvāsā when pursued by the discus. Exhausted, distraught, fearful and grieving, he wandered through Brahmā's realm, Śiva's city and every world, but none offered him a seat: who can protect an enemy of Rāma? For such a person mother becomes death, father becomes Yama, nectar becomes poison, a friend acts like a hundred enemies, and the celestial Gaṅgā becomes the Vaitaraṇī; indeed, one opposed to Rāma finds the whole world hotter than fire. Seeing Jayanta distraught, compassionate Nārada sent him at once to Rāma and told him to cry for the protector of those who surrender. Terrified and desperate, Jayanta clasped Rāma's feet and begged for rescue, confessing that in his dullness he had failed to recognize the Lord's immeasurable power and had now come for refuge after reaping his own deed's fruit. Hearing the sufferer's plea, compassionate Rāma spared him after taking one eye. Though delusion had driven him to enmity and death was deserved, Rāma released him out of tenderness—for who is compassionate like Rāma?

While dwelling at Citrakūṭa, Rāma performed many deeds equal to the nectar of the Vedas. Then he reflected that a crowd would gather once everyone knew him there. Taking leave of all the sages, the two brothers departed with Sītā. When the Lord reached Atri's hermitage, the great sage heard and rejoiced. His body thrilled, Atri ran out; seeing Rāma approach eagerly, he prostrated and embraced him, bathing both brothers in tears of love. His eyes were soothed by Rāma's beauty; he respectfully brought them into his hermitage, worshipped them, spoke gracious words, and offered roots and fruits pleasing to the Lord. When the Lord was seated, the supremely wise and accomplished sage gazed to his heart's content upon his splendour, joined his palms, and began a hymn of praise.

I bow to the tender-natured, compassionate lover of devotees, and worship his lotus feet, which bestow his own abode on those free from desire. I adore the perfectly lovely dark-hued Lord, Mount Mandara for the ocean of becoming, whose eyes are full-blown lotuses and who frees us from pride and other faults. His long arms are valiant and his majesty immeasurable; he bears quiver, bow and arrows and is Lord of the three worlds. Ornament of the solar race and breaker of Śiva's bow, he delights eminent sages and saints and destroys the hosts of the gods' enemies. Honoured by Śiva, the foe of Kāma, and served by Brahmā and the other gods, he is the embodiment of pure consciousness and removes every defect. I bow to Lakṣmī's lord, maker of happiness and refuge of the good; I worship him with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa—the beloved younger brother of Indra's son. People who worship at your feet without envy do not fall into the ocean of becoming, crowded with waves of disputation. Solitary dwellers who joyfully reject the senses and their objects and worship for liberation attain their own true state. I worship that one wondrous Lord: desireless sovereign, all-pervading master, teacher of the world, eternal, the fourth state alone. Beloved of loving devotion and very hard for false yogins to attain, he is a wish-fulfilling tree for his devotees, impartial, and readily served every day. I bow to the incomparable, beautiful king, husband of Sītā, daughter of Earth. Be gracious: I bow to you; grant me devotion to your lotus feet. Those who respectfully recite this hymn reach your abode endowed with devotion to you—of this there is no doubt.

entries.meaning: The modest, virtuous Sītā clasped Anasūyā's feet and met her again. The sage's wife rejoiced greatly, blessed her, seated her nearby, and dressed her in divine, spotless garments and ornaments that ever remained fresh. Speaking sweetly and gently, Anasūyā used the occasion to explain a woman's marital dharma. ‘Mother, father and brother are benefactors, princess, but their gifts are limited; a husband gives without limit, so a woman who will not serve him is base. Fortitude, dharma, friendship and a wife—these four are tested in adversity. Even if a husband is old, ill, witless, poor, blind, deaf, irascible or utterly wretched, a wife who insults him suffers many torments in Yama's city. Her one dharma, vow and rule is love for her husband's feet in body, speech and mind. The Vedas, Purāṇas and saints describe four kinds of devoted wives. The highest holds in her mind that no man but her husband exists, even in dream. The middling sees another's husband as her own brother, father or son according to his age. She who remains within family propriety through reflection on dharma is lower; scripture calls one who abstains only from lack of opportunity or fear the lowest. A wife who deceives her husband and loves another falls into Raurava hell for a hundred cosmic ages; for a moment's pleasure she earns suffering through a hundred crore births—who is more corrupt? A woman can attain the highest destiny without toil, yet she abandons marital fidelity and embraces deceit. Wherever one hostile to her husband is born, she becomes a widow in youth. Though naturally impure, a woman serving her husband attains an auspicious destiny; the four Vedas still sing the fame of Tulasī, who is dear to Hari. Sītā, women will remember your name and practise fidelity. Because Rāma holds you dearer than life, I have told this account for the world's good.’

Hearing Anasūyā, Jānakī felt supreme joy and respectfully bowed her head at her feet. Rāma then asked the sage for permission to go to another forest, requesting his constant grace and love for him as a servant. Hearing the Lord, bearer of dharma's burden, the wise sage lovingly replied: ‘Rāma, you—whose grace Brahmā, Śiva, Sanaka and every seeker of the highest truth desire—have spoken tenderly to me, your desireless beloved, calling yourself friend of the helpless. Now I understand Śrī's strategy: I abandoned every god and worshipped you, who have no equal or superior. How could the character of such a one be otherwise? How can I tell you to go, Master? Tell me yourself, Lord, for you know the heart.’ Saying this and gazing upon the Lord, the steadfast sage's eyes streamed and his body thrilled. Filled utterly with love, his body thrilled; fixing his lotus eyes and face upon the Lord beyond mind, knowledge and attributes, he said, ‘What need have I seen for ritual recitation or austerity? Through all recitation, yoga and dharma a person receives incomparable devotion; Tulasī, Rāma's servant, sings day and night the purifying deeds of Raghu's hero. Rāma's lovely fame destroys the stain of Kali, disciplines the mind, and is the root of happiness. Rāma remains gracious to those who hear it respectfully. This difficult age is a treasury of impurity, with neither dharma, knowledge, yoga nor recitation; those wise people abandon every other reliance and worship Rāma.’
